questions.question: A relation R on set X is reflexive if

answers.a: (a, a) in R ∀ a in X
answers.b: aRb implies bRa, ∀ a, b in X
answers.c: (a, b) in R ∀ a,b in X
answers.d: If (a, b) in R and (b, c) in R then, (a, c) in R, ∀ a, b, c in X

explanations.a: Correct! A relation is reflexive if every element is related to itself. This means for every element a in set X, (a,a) must be in relation R. For example, if X = {1,2,3}, then (1,1), (2,2), and (3,3) must all be in R for it to be reflexive.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This is actually the definition of a symmetric relation, not reflexivity. Reflexivity only deals with how an element relates to itself, not how pairs of different elements relate to each other.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This would mean every possible pair of elements must be related, which is too strong. Reflexivity only requires elements to be related to themselves, not to every other element.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This is the definition of transitivity, which deals with chains of relations. Reflexivity is simpler - it only requires each element to be related to itself.

questions.question: A relation R on set X is transitive if

answers.a: (a, a) in R ∀ a in X
answers.b: aRb implies bRa, ∀ a, b in X
answers.c: (a, b) in R ∀ a,b in X
answers.d: If (a, b) in R and (b, c) in R then, (a, c) in R, ∀ a, b, c in X

explanations.a: Incorrect. This is the definition of reflexivity. Transitivity deals with how chains of relations behave, not how elements relate to themselves.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This defines symmetry, where if a is related to b, then b must be related to a. Transitivity instead deals with chains of relations.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This would mean every possible pair must be related, which is much stronger than transitivity. A relation can be transitive without including every possible pair.
explanations.d: Correct! Transitivity means that if we have a chain of relations - a related to b, and b related to c - then a must be related to c. For example, if 'is greater than' is transitive, then if 5 > 3 and 3 > 1, we know 5 > 1.

questions.question: A relation R is symmetric if

answers.a: (a, a) in R ∀ a in X
answers.b: aRb implies bRa, ∀ a, b in X
answers.c: (a, b) in R ∀ a,b in X
answers.d: If (a, b) in R and (b, c) in R then, (a, c) in R, ∀ a, b, c in X

explanations.a: Incorrect. This defines reflexivity, which requires elements to be related to themselves. Symmetry instead deals with pairs of elements and their reciprocal relationships.
explanations.b: Correct! A relation is symmetric if whenever a is related to b, b must also be related to a. For example, 'is sibling of' is symmetric because if Alice is Bob's sibling, then Bob is also Alice's sibling.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This would require every possible pair of elements to be related, which is much stronger than symmetry. A relation can be symmetric without including all possible pairs.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This defines transitivity, which deals with chains of relations. Symmetry is about reciprocal relationships between pairs of elements.

questions.question: In a Hasse diagram of a partially ordered set, which edges can be omitted without losing information about the ordering?

answers.b: Edges that can be inferred through transitivity

explanations.a: Correct but incomplete. While reflexive edges (loops) are indeed omitted in Hasse diagrams, this is not the only type of edge that can be omitted.
explanations.b: Correct! In a Hasse diagram, if we have edges from a to b and b to c, we can omit the edge from a to c since it can be inferred through transitivity. This makes the diagram cleaner and easier to read.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Incomparable elements don't have edges between them in the first place, so there are no such edges to omit.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Partial orders are antisymmetric, not symmetric, so there are no symmetric edges to omit in a proper partial order.

questions.question: Given a partially ordered set (X, ≤), an element m ∈ X is called maximal if:

answers.a: For all x ∈ X, x ≤ m
answers.b: For all x ∈ X, m ≤ x
answers.c: For all x ∈ X, if m ≤ x then x = m
answers.d: For all x ∈ X, if x ≤ m then x = m

explanations.a: Incorrect. This defines a greatest element, which is stronger than a maximal element. A maximal element doesn't need to be greater than all other elements.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This would mean m is the least element, which is the opposite of what we want for a maximal element.
explanations.c: Correct! A maximal element m has no element greater than itself. If any element x is greater than or equal to m, it must be equal to m.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This would mean m is minimal (no elements below it) rather than maximal (no elements above it).

questions.question: Which property distinguishes a partial order from an equivalence relation?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Both partial orders and equivalence relations are reflexive - this is a shared property.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Both partial orders and equivalence relations are transitive - this is a shared property.
explanations.c: Correct! The key difference is that partial orders are antisymmetric (if a ≤ b and b ≤ a, then a = b) while equivalence relations are symmetric (if a ~ b then b ~ a).
explanations.d: Incorrect. There is a clear distinguishing property - the presence of antisymmetry versus symmetry.

questions.question: In a lattice (L, ≤), what is true about the meet (∧) and join (∨) of any two elements a, b ∈ L?

answers.a: a ∧ b is always less than both a and b; a ∨ b is always greater than both a and b
answers.b: a ∧ b is the unique greatest lower bound; a ∨ b is the unique least upper bound
answers.c: a ∧ b = b ∧ a and a ∨ b = b ∨ a

explanations.a: Correct but incomplete. While this is true, it doesn't capture all the important properties of meets and joins.
explanations.b: Correct but incomplete. This is a key property but doesn't mention the commutativity of these operations.
explanations.c: Correct but incomplete. While commutativity is important, it misses the crucial ordering properties.
explanations.d: Correct! All these properties are essential for lattices: meets are greatest lower bounds, joins are least upper bounds, and both operations are commutative.

questions.question: Given a Hasse diagram, what can we conclude if there exists no path between elements a and b?

answers.a: a and b must be equal elements
answers.b: a and b are incomparable elements
answers.c: Either a < b or b < a must be true
answers.d: a and b cannot be in the same partially ordered set

explanations.a: Incorrect. Equal elements would be represented by the same point in a Hasse diagram.
explanations.b: Correct! When no path exists between elements in a Hasse diagram, it means neither a ≤ b nor b ≤ a holds - the definition of incomparable elements.
explanations.c: Incorrect. If either relation held, there would be a path (either upward or downward) between a and b.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Elements in the same partially ordered set can be incomparable - this is what makes it a partial (not total) order.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a chain and an antichain in a partially ordered set?

answers.a: Every element must belong to either a chain or an antichain
answers.b: The intersection of a chain and an antichain can contain at most one element
answers.c: The union of all maximal chains equals the union of all maximal antichains
answers.d: Chains and antichains must have the same size in any finite partial order

explanations.a: Incorrect. An element can belong to both a chain and an antichain, or to multiple chains or antichains.
explanations.b: Correct! Since elements in a chain are comparable and elements in an antichain are incomparable, their intersection can't contain more than one element - otherwise it would contradict one of these properties.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This is not generally true - the structure of chains and antichains can be quite different.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The sizes of chains and antichains can be very different; this relationship is studied in Dilworth's theorem.
